claims.text: Percolating chemical short-range-order clusters cause a non-monotonic transition in the thermal conductivity of single-phase bcc refractory high-entropy alloys.
Before percolation, isolated SRO clusters act as phonon-scattering centers and reduce thermal conductivity.
After percolation, connected ordered clusters form coherent phonon-transport channels that increase conductivity above the random-solid-solution baseline.
The initial HfNbTaTiZr-like alloy is a single-phase bcc random solid solution with negligible SRO.
The random solid solution has high force-constant fluctuations and low lattice thermal conductivity because of strong phonon scattering.
Annealing at 800–1200 K can induce equilibrium SRO in the target bcc refractory alloy.
Cooling after annealing allows the SRO clusters to percolate into a connected network.
Reliable modeling requires a potential-energy surface that captures chemical-ordering energetics, whereas standard pair potentials may fail to predict SRO evolution.
Moment Tensor Potentials or DFT-derived cluster expansions can capture the ordering energetics required for modeling SRO.
The SRO state remains stable above 800 K while the alloy retains a single-phase bcc structure.
Phonon mean free paths in the operating regime are comparable to an SRO-cluster length scale of approximately 1–2 nm.
A percolating SRO network reduces force-constant variance along selected crystallographic directions.
FeCoCrMnNi and Ni-based alloys provide precedent for disorder-associated phonon broadening and reduced thermal conductivity.
Serial, parallel, and Maxwell–Eucken mixing models predict a monotonic decrease or linear interpolation of conductivity and cannot reproduce the proposed percolative enhancement.
Thermal conductivity should display a peak or inflection as SRO volume fraction or annealing time crosses the percolation regime.
The mechanism requires SRO percolation without phase separation or precipitation.
W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf provides precedent for high-temperature stability without substantial precipitation or grain coarsening.
The percolative mechanism requires phonon wavelengths to be comparable to the SRO-cluster size.
A connectivity value greater than 0.5 constitutes the relevant SRO percolation threshold.
The coherent-channel mechanism predicts reduced phonon scattering rates within percolated ordered regions, detectable through phonon-linewidth measurements.
